question: What prevents a half-written anonymized corpus from looking ready?
related_questions: What happens if the process crashes mid-publish?
Why is report.json the readiness marker?

bullets: Delete existing report.json before touching corpus.
Fsync the output directory after removal.
steps.spoken: Step one: nothing is allowed to look ready until it actually is. Before the pipeline touches a single output file, it deletes the old report — the file that tells every downstream system, this result is finished. Think of pulling the done sticker off the box before you open it. Then it force syncs the directory, so the deletion itself survives a crash. Why does the order matter? If we crash halfway through writing, there is no report at all, so nothing downstream can ever mistake a half written corpus for a finished one. You can follow this at the top of the publish function in pipeline dot py. And the debugger stop proves the report is the very last thing written — only after every byte is in place.
steps.title: Invalidate stale readiness

bullets: Recompute the staging corpus digest.
Reject if staged bytes changed after verification.
steps.proof_boundary: Detects staging mutation, not undeclared sensitive data.
steps.spoken: Step two: prove the bytes you verified are the bytes you ship. After anonymization, the pipeline seals a fingerprint of the staged output. Right before publishing, it recomputes that fingerprint and compares the two. If anything changed in between — even one byte — the publish is rejected outright. It is like sealing an envelope, then checking the seal is unbroken before you mail it. Same file, pipeline dot py — the seal check sits just before the swap. One honest limit: this catches changes after verification. It cannot know about sensitive data nobody told it about in the first place.
steps.title: Seal verified bytes

teleprompter_points: The output is not ready until report.json exists.
The old readiness marker is removed before corpus replacement.
The staged corpus is re-hashed after verification and before publish.
report.json is fsynced and atomically renamed last.
title: Fail-closed atomic publication writes report.json last

bullets: A phone stored as an integer is the same phone.
str(5551234567) contains the policy string, so it is replaced.
1e20 expands to 100000000000000000000 so scientific notation cannot hide it.
steps.proof_boundary: Covers JSON string/int/float and SQLite TEXT/INTEGER/REAL; BLOB fails closed.
steps.source_explanation: _replace_json stringifies int/float scalars (with integral/decimal expansion) before matching, so a sensitive value is caught in any JSON/SQLite scalar type.
steps.spoken: Step one, the actual fix. The trial was lost because a phone number stored as a number slipped past a matcher that only understood text. The fix is simple to say and easy to miss: match the value, not the way it happens to be written. Before any number is passed through, we turn it into its canonical text form and run the same policy check. An integer phone, a float, scientific notation — all become the one value they represent, and all get anonymized.
steps.title: Match the value, not the spelling

bullets: The original verifier shared the same string-only blind spot as the transform.
Now it scans values, views, schema DDL, header integers, and raw bytes independently.
If the transform ever regresses, the verifier still fails closed.
steps.proof_boundary: The verifier reads the staged output fresh; it does not reuse the transform's matcher or data generator.
steps.source_explanation: _count in verification.py independently NFC-normalizes and scans; iter_searchable_text scans every table cell, materialized views, all schema DDL, and every SQLite header integer, plus a whole-file raw-byte pass.
steps.spoken: Step two, why we can trust it now. The old safety net had the exact same hole as the thing it was checking — both only looked at text. That is why nothing failed closed. The verifier is now genuinely independent: it re-derives what should be gone and scans the released file every way a value can hide — table cells, views, schema text, the SQLite header, and the raw bytes themselves. Two layers, no shared assumption.
steps.title: An independent verifier that shares no assumptions

bullets: The real root cause was authoring the check from the code's behavior.
Now the check reads policy.json directly and is wired into verify.sh.
15 holes verified through docker run; each retained as a regression.
steps.proof_boundary: The gate reads policy.json; a dependency probe proves the result depends on the spec, not a hardcoded list.
steps.source_explanation: scripts/spec_derived_check.py reads the values from policy.json and asserts none survives; setup-project now requires the brief as a declared input and the immutable goal to carry the spec.
steps.spoken: Step three, the lesson that outlasts this one bug. The deeper mistake was writing the test to match what the code already did, instead of what the client's spec required. Now the acceptance check reads the policy file itself and asserts every listed value is gone from the output. And it is proven the honest way — through the real Docker command the evaluator runs, fifteen distinct leak paths, each one a permanent regression test.
steps.title: The check comes from the spec, not the code

teleprompter_points: The disqualifier: a phone stored as a JSON/SQLite integer passed the string-only matcher.
Root cause: the acceptance check was authored from the code's behavior, not derived from the delivered policy.json.
Fix: match the value in any representation, in the transform AND an independent verifier that does not share the producer's assumptions.
Every hole is verified through the real docker run and retained as a regression.
title: Value-scoped anonymization and representation hardening

steps.spoken: Start at intake. The pipeline accepts a bundle only if policy dot json and corpus slash are ordinary files and directories, then it inventories exactly what it received before any output can become ready.

bullets: Write anonymized files into private staging.
Replace policy values across supported scalar representations.
Keep unfinished output away from the readiness marker.
steps.proof_boundary: Transforms values covered by the delivered policy and supported formats.
steps.source_explanation: transform_file and the format-specific replacers write anonymized records into the staging corpus, including scalar value handling for JSON and SQLite surfaces.
steps.spoken: Next, every supported file is anonymized into a private staging directory. This is where the value-scoped fix matters: a phone stored as a number is still treated as the policy value, not as a harmless integer.
steps.title: Transform into a staged anonymized corpus

bullets: Run an independent verifier over staged output.
Reject if source files changed during processing.
Hash the verified staged corpus before publish.
steps.proof_boundary: The seal proves the verified staged bytes are the bytes sent to publish.
steps.source_explanation: After verify_corpus passes, run_pipeline rejects source drift, computes sealed_digest over the staged corpus, and passes that digest into _publish.
steps.spoken: Then the pipeline verifies before release. It scans the staged output, checks the input did not change underneath it, and seals a digest of the exact bytes that passed verification.
steps.title: Verify and seal what will be released

bullets: Remove stale report.json before changing output.
Recheck the sealed digest immediately before publish.
Write report.json last as the only ready signal.
steps.source_explanation: _publish removes stale report.json, rechecks sealed_digest, swaps corpus into place, and atomically writes report.json last as the readiness marker.
steps.spoken: Finally, release is report-last. The old report is removed first, the sealed digest is checked again, the corpus is swapped into place, and only then is report dot json written as the ready signal.
steps.title: Publish corpus first, report.json last

teleprompter_points: The input bundle is accepted only after policy.json and corpus/ pass preflight.
Each supported file is transformed into a private staging corpus.
Verification scans the staged corpus against the policy-derived sensitive values.
The verified corpus is sealed, published, and only then report.json marks the release ready.
title: Input dataset to ready anonymized release
